newsitem.title: USA: U.S. futures exchanges, regulators face off over reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. futures exchanges, regulators face off over reforms.

text.p: The biggest U.S. futures exchanges pleaded on Tuesday for the government to stop "micro-managing" futures contracts and giving overseas exchanges a competitive edge.
"The top exchanges in the world will be on foreign shores unless we get some kind of regulatory relief," said John Sandner, head of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

Sandner and his counterparts with the Chicago Board of Trade, the New York Mercantile Exchange and New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange found a sympathetic audience when they testified before a House Agriculture subcommittee.
The panel is considering a controversial bill that would strip the Commodity Futures Trading Commission of much of its regulatory power.

The proposed legislation has bipartisan support and would exempt so-called "professional markets" from various U.S. regulations, including segregation of customer funds, extensive record-keeping and sometimes lengthy procedures to win approval for new contracts.
The LIFFE in London claims to be the second-biggest futures exchange in the world, overtaking the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

Some U.S. customers and traders have moved their business to London because of less paperwork required by the exchange and its ability to introduce new contracts swiftly, said Sandner, who said the CFTC was "micro-managing" U.S. exchanges.
Five years ago, NYMEX had about 50 percent of the copper futures market in the world. But that has dwindled to less than 10 percent today, said Daniel Rappaport, chairman of NYMEX.
"Soon there is going to be nothing left to regulate because the market is going to go overseas," he said.

Members of a House Agriculture subcommittee, chaired by Representative Thomas Ewing (R-Ill.), expressed concern at the loss of business on U.S. futures markets, saying regulators want to balance the needs of traders with protection for the public.
The exchanges have lobbied in favour of the legislation, demanding regulatory relief to compete with fast-growing futures exchanges in London and other cities.

CFTC Commissioner Brooksley Born, who also testified, reminded the subcommittee about the dangers of market manipulation by a Sumitomo trader in copper last year, the Hunt Brothers' squeeze on the silver market in the 1980s and other futures problems in recent years.
The CFTC contends that if the so-called professional market is exempted from regulation -- comprising about 90 percent of all U.S. futures traded -- the market will be vulnerable to manipulation.
Currently, the agency requires the exchanges to collect daily data about large positions in the market, segregate client funds and maintain an audit trail of trades, among other regulations.
"This legislation would result in U.S. futures exchanges having less government regulation than any other futures exchange in the world," Born said.
The proposed cut in government regulation also comes at a time when U.S. farmers and ranchers are being encouraged to turn to the futures market, she said.

Under last year's farm legislation phasing out the longstanding system of price supports, U.S. farmers and ranchers are being encouraged by the Agriculture Department to investigate futures and other risk management techniques.

The two Chicago exchanges tried to allay the concern of the subcommittee over farmers and ranchers in the futures market by saying they did not plan to include agricultural futures markets in the trading arenas exempted from regulation.
"No one would be hurt by this (legislation)," Sandner said in response to questioning by Representative Jerry Moran (R-Kan.). "These are customers with large accounts who want less regulation."
But a two-tier market could drain liquidity from the regulated side, the CFTC contends, making it less effective as a place for farmers to hedge crop risks.
